title: Understanding the Gift Card Fallacy
subtitle: how we can share the pie without shrinking it

lines.text: Almost every argument about the economy comes down to the same tug of war.
Grow the pie, or share the pie.
Sharing matters because a dollar means more to someone who has fewer of them.
Doubling your money feels about the same whether you go from a thousand dollars to two thousand, or from a million to two million.
So take Alice and Bob, with five thousand dollars each. Now give Bob one thousand and Alice nineteen thousand. Twice the money, and less total happiness.
The Schöntrup index scores a whole society this way: the average logarithm of everyone's income. It rewards growing the pie and sharing it at the same time.
lines.say: The Shurn-troop index scores a whole society this way: the average logarithm of everyone's income. It rewards growing the pie and sharing it at the same time.

lines.text: That's the case for redistribution. The trouble is the tools we usually reach for.
Steep tax brackets. Rent control. Minimum wages. Food stamps. Each one shrinks the pie a little.
Economists call that lost value deadweight loss: wealth that simply vanishes.
So the debate turns into a gamble. Will a bigger pie make up for less sharing? Maybe. Maybe not.
But there's a mistake hiding inside that whole framing. Call it the gift card fallacy.
Say I spend a hundred dollars on a gift card for you, and you'd only pay seventy for it. Thirty dollars just went up in smoke.

Now look at the safety net. Food stamps: a grocery gift card. Housing vouchers: a rent gift card. Free public parking: a gift card for drivers, paid for by everyone. Even the public library is a gift card for books.
And rent control? A thousand-dollar gift card for one tenant, funded by a thousand-dollar tax on one landlord who happened to own that building.
Here's the good news. Economics already has a theorem for this: the second welfare theorem.
Pick whatever amount of sharing you want. A little, or a lot. You can get there without shrinking the pie.
Tax things that can't shrink when you tax them, hand people cash, and let markets handle the rest.
Things nobody can be fenced out of, like national defense, still get funded directly. Nearly everything else? Cash.
Start with land. Nobody can make more of it, so taxing its value doesn't shrink anything.
Next, pollution. Taxing it actually grows the pie, because polluters finally pay for the damage they cause.
Need more? Add one flat tax rate on income. No brackets.
Then split the money equally. Every citizen gets the same check.

Try a forty percent flat rate with a ten thousand dollar dividend. Earn twelve thousand, and you take home seventeen thousand two hundred. Earn a million, and you pay thirty-nine percent. As progressive as any bracket system, with no brackets at all.
So stop arguing about how much to share. Whatever amount you choose, cash delivers it cheaper.
The poor end up with more. Taxpayers pay less. At the same time.
A free-market welfare state. Just give people money.
